title: Chapter 3: Form 9
content: The row across takes eleven minutes and costs her both gloves.

Second Crossing is fourteen feet of aluminum with a flat bottom and a thirty-year-old outboard she does not use, because the river is still high and a motor is a good way to lose an argument with a standing wave. Wren rows. The current pushes her downstream a hundred yards, and she comes in under the west ramp and ties to the iron ring, and by then her palms are burning inside the gloves.

The ferry is closed. The Authority put a notice on the east ramp on Sunday afternoon, a sheet of paper in a plastic sleeve, and the notice says the crossing is suspended pending inspection of the cable and the drum. It does not mention insurance. It does not have to. Hollis said the policy lapsed in June and a boat without a policy is a boat that cannot legally carry a soul, and the county does not care how many people need to get to work on Monday.
So she rows, and she is at 400 Third Street at eight fifty-two, and the Annex is exactly what she has driven past for twenty-four years without once going in.

It is brown brick with a flat roof and a row of windows that do not open, and it was built in 1961, the same year as Kettler Gate, by the same people, out of the same budget. There is a plaque by the door with a blueprint etched into it. There is a wheelchair ramp that is too steep. There is a sign that says BASIN AUTHORITY, DISTRICT 4, and under that, in smaller letters, a sentence about the stewardship of the Sable River Basin that somebody in Columbus wrote and nobody here has ever read.
Inside, the carpet is the color of wet cardboard and the light is fluorescent, and one tube in the ceiling is dying with a tick every four seconds.

There is a door at the end of the room with a plastic plaque that says PUBLIC READING ROOM, and through its window she can see a long table, two chairs, and a copier with a coin box on it. The door is unlocked. Nobody is in there. It is the only part of the building with a window that opens.

Three windows in a counter. One is open. There is a brass bell on the sill with a sign that says RING FOR SERVICE, and a row of orange plastic chairs bolted to the floor, and six people sitting in them.
Wren takes a number from the machine. The machine is the kind that dispenses a paper ticket, and the ticket says 07, and the sign above the counter says NOW SERVING 03.

She sits. She has a folder on her knee with the form in it that she printed at the library on Sunday afternoon, all four pages, because she wanted to read it before she filled it out. She has read it eleven times. She can recite section six in her sleep.
The woman beside her is holding a dock permit and a photograph of a dock.
"Are you filing or appealing?" the woman says.
"Filing."
"Filing's faster." The woman looks at the counter. "My husband says filing's faster."
At eight fifty-eight Hollis Drane comes in through the back with a travel mug and a canvas bag, and he sees her, and his face does something complicated and quickly put away.

He goes behind the counter. He turns on a lamp. He takes off his coat and hangs it on a hook and puts on a cardigan that was already there, which means the cardigan lives at the Annex and Hollis lives somewhere else entirely.

At nine oh one he presses a button and the sign changes to 04, and the woman with the dock goes up, and nobody rings the bell, because the bell is for when there is nobody at the window, and there is always somebody at the window.
At nine twenty-six the sign says 07.
Wren stands up and goes to the window.
"Morning, Wren," Hollis says.
"Morning."
He waits. He has a pen already in his hand, and a stamp pad, and a stack of forms squared up on the blotter, and he is ready for a fence permit.
"I need a Form 9," she says.
The pen stops. "Who told you about Form 9?"
"You did. Yesterday, at the diner."
He looks like a man who has been caught being helpful. "Certificate of Loss."
"Certificate of Loss." She puts the library printout on the counter, face up. "I know what it is. I need the office copy, the carbonless one, because the library one isn't the one the county takes."

Hollis looks at the printout for a while. Then he goes to the back and comes out with a pad of forms, and he sets it down and squares it up with the others without meaning to, and slides one copy across.
It is four pages, stapled, on paper the color of a paper bag. The top right corner says REV. 11/19 and the bottom left says BASIN AUTHORITY D4.
"Four dollars," Hollis says. "There's no fee for a death. It's four dollars for the copies."
She pays four dollars. He gives her a receipt from a receipt book, handwritten, and she folds it and puts it in the folder and does not throw it away.
She fills it in at the counter with the pen on the chain, because the pen on the chain is the only pen the Annex provides, and the chain is short, and she has to lean in.
Page one. Decedent. Aubrey, Elias Wade. Date of birth, 4 March 1948. Age, 78. Residence, 9 Ferry Lane, Kestrel Bend. Occupation, ferry operator. Years in occupation, fifty-one.
Page two. Date of loss, 12 September 2026. Time, 22:04. Place, Sable River, Mile 9, east ramp, Kestrel Bend, Marrow County. Means, cable ferry, privately operated. Persons present, nine.
Page three. Informant. Aubrey, Wren. Relationship, granddaughter. Address, same. Telephone, the house line, which she has to think about because nobody has called it since Friday.
Page four has the office boxes and the routing block, and above them, section six, which is four lines long and has a box beside it the size of a postage stamp.
CAUSE, AS CERTIFIED.
There is a smaller line under it that says attach certification if available, and a smaller line under that which says if not available, state cause and await district review.
Wren writes, in her own hand, in that small box, the word drowned.
She writes it small and clear. Then she sits back and looks at it, and it is the first time in her life she has been glad of a word.

Hollis has been watching her write. He does not take the form. His pen is in his hand and it is not moving, and it hovers over the page the way a wasp hovers over a window, and she can see the nib tremble with the effort of not touching the paper.
"That's not a certification," he says.
"It's the cause."
"It's your opinion of the cause. Section six wants it certified."
"By the district. Which is the Basin Authority. Which is you."

"I am the town clerk at a district annex, Wren. I take forms and I stamp forms. I don't certify anything. Certification comes out of Columbus." He says Columbus the way people here say the capital, as if it were a different country with a border. "I can take the form. I can't certify it."
"Then where does it go?"
"It goes in the mail."
"To who?"
"To the district registrar."
"And the district registrar is the same office that ran the release."
Hollis does not answer that. His jaw works. "The classification is on the incident file. I don't write the classification."
"Then show me the line."
"What line?"
"The line that says an uncertified Form 9 can't be accepted at a district annex. Show me. It's in the manual. You have the manual. It's behind you in a green binder with a broken spine."
Hollis turns and looks at the binder as if it has said something rude.

He takes the binder down. He opens it on the counter and turns the pages, and the pages are in plastic sleeves and some of them are yellow, and he turns them twice, and then he stops, and his finger is on a paragraph, and he reads it, and his mouth moves.
"I don't have a line," he says.
"No."

"There's a line that says the clerk shall forward the form. It doesn't say I can refuse it. It just says the form is not complete until the certification is entered." He looks up. "So it's incomplete. It's not refused. It's incomplete."
"Then take it, and give me a duplicate with today's date on it, and write on the duplicate that you received it and what time."

He could say no. She watches him decide not to. It is not courage on his part and it is not kindness. It is the ordinary fear of a man who has been a clerk for thirty years and knows that a date stamp is a fact and a fact is the one thing that cannot be argued with later.
He takes the form. He stamps the yellow duplicate with the date stamp, 14 SEP 2026, and writes 9:31 in the box by hand, and initials it H.D.
He pushes the duplicate across. Wren folds it into the folder with the receipt.
Then he takes the original and the two carbons and goes through the door behind the counter, and she can hear a drawer open, wood on wood, and the sound of paper going into paper.
He is gone long enough for the woman with the dock permit to come back and ask whether the counter is closed.
He comes back out. He has his pen again. He does not look at her.
"Where did you put it?" Wren says.
"In the pending file."
"Which is where?"
"Second desk," he says, and then, because he is a clerk and clerks are precise, and because he is tired, "bottom left."
She looks past him at the second desk, at the drawer, at the brown metal front of it, and she memorizes the drawer the way she memorized the second rung and the plate that says nine.

"Draper telephoned me at eight," Hollis says. "He's got him in the back room and he can hold him, but he can't do a service without a burial permit, and I can't issue a burial permit without a certificate. Thirty years he's had that funeral home. He said he's never had a body he couldn't bury."
"So he sits in the back room."
"He sits in the back room," Hollis says.
"When will it move?" she says.

Hollis puts his hand flat on the counter. He is not being cruel. That is the awful thing, she thinks, he is not being cruel at all, he is being a man at the end of a Monday morning telling a girl the truth and wishing the truth were better.
"Maybe tomorrow," he says.
The bell over the window rings.
A man in a seed cap steps up with a form for a shed, and Hollis takes it, and stamps it, and the stamp comes down on the shed with a sound like a door closing.
highlight: Wren rows the high river to the Annex and files Form 9, and Hollis drops it in the drawer.
